justification: This is a genuine, well-researched contribution, not a repackaging of the standard async/await tutorial. The strongest evidence of originality is the deadlock section: I fetched Stephen Cleary's canonical 'Don't Block on Async Code' post (the most-cited explanation of this exact failure) and confirmed it explains the .Result deadlock entirely in prose with two short, non-runnable snippets and no custom SynchronizationContext implementation. This article instead builds a real, runnable ExclusiveContext : SynchronizationContext (a BlockingCollection-backed single-thread pump), reproduces the deadlock with a 2-second timeout proving the hang, and then flips exactly one line (ConfigureAwait(false)) to show the fix removing it — a materially deeper and more rigorous treatment than the source it most resembles conceptually. The hand-written state-machine sketch (AddOneStateMachine/MoveNext), the SynchronizationContext.Current experiment, the WhenAll exception-aggregation demo, the cancellation walkthrough, and the ValueTask allocation measurements are all original constructions with original variable names and framing; none read as lifted or closely paraphrased from any source I checked. I verified all 11 cited sources are real and, by live-fetching seven of them (await operator, TAP overview, ValueTask Struct, ValueTask<TResult>, async-scenarios, Task.WhenAll, the 2011 MSDN Magazine SynchronizationContext piece by Stephen Cleary, ConfigureAwait FAQ, How Async/Await Really Works), confirmed every direct quotation in the article is verbatim-accurate and attached to the sentence it actually supports: the await-operator quote, the TAP 'doesn't force a method to run asynchronously' quote, the async-void 'can't be caught outside of that method' / 'difficult to test' / 'negative side effects' triad, the WhenAll 'aggregation of the set of unwrapped exceptions' sentence, and the three SynchronizationContext behavior quotes (WinForms/WPF exclusivity, ASP.NET per-request serialization, console apps having only the default context) all match the live pages exactly, including the correct human author (Stephen Cleary) of the archived 2011 piece. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/csharp-dotnet/async-await.md` passes exactly as claimed (PASS, blocks=36, executed=19). The toolchain statement ('.NET 10.0.12 on Windows 11, x64, on a Core i7-11700K') is correctly placed beside the first timed measurement in 'A loop that ties up its thread,' not in the opener, matching the binding rule. Structure is distinct from its only sibling, value-types-vs-reference-types.md: none of the nine headings in either article repeat, neither uses boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion headings, and the four exercises (predict-it, find-the-bug, extend-it, measure-it) are genuinely different forms — the predict-it exercise correctly withholds its output panel until the solution, per the binding 'do not give away exercises' rule. The async-void crash demo reuses a child-process technique that does exist in operating-systems/processes-and-threads.md ('A crash takes the whole process, and stops at its edge'): both spawn a self-referencing child process via ProcessStartInfo with RedirectStandardOutput/Error and inspect the exit code and first stderr line. This is legitimate reuse of an engineering pattern across pillars, not copied prose — the two demos illustrate different mechanisms (an unhandled exception on a raw Thread vs. one thrown from an async void continuation with a try/catch that provably does not catch it) and the surrounding explanatory text is entirely distinct. The ValueTask 'measure it' exercise is honest, hedged methodology, not an inflated claim: it explicitly distinguishes the hand-constructed ValueTask<string> (0 B regardless of Optimize) from an async ValueTask<T> method (64 B under debug codegen, 0 B optimized) and states plainly that 'the saving is real, but it is not automatic just because the return type changed' rather than presenting a single flattering number. Two issues keep this off a 9.5+: two of the eleven listed sources (the 'Foreground and background threads' doc and the 'Understanding the Whys, Whats, and Whens of ValueTask' devblog post) are never cited inline anywhere in the body, which the editorial brief's binding pilot-round lessons calls out explicitly as its own finding; and the ValueTask Struct quote ('the default choice for any asynchronous method... should be Task') elides, via its ellipsis, the qualifying clause 'that does not return a result' from the live source, which on that specific page refers to the non-generic ValueTask rather than the ValueTask<TResult> the article is discussing — the claim is still true (I confirmed the ValueTask<TResult> page independently states 'the default choice for any asynchronous method should be to return a Task or Task<TResult>'), but the citation as constructed doesn't quite support the generic-type claim it's attached to as tightly as it appears to.

issues.location: Front matter `sources` list, entries 'Foreground and background threads' (learn.microsoft.com/.../foreground-and-background-threads) and 'Understanding the Whys, Whats, and Whens of ValueTask' (devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/understanding-the-whys-whats-and-whens-of-valuetask)
issues.problem: Neither source is cited inline anywhere in the article body (confirmed by searching for both URLs and for related terms like 'foreground'/'IsBackground' in the running text). The editorial brief's binding lessons state: 'A source in the list that is never cited inline... is a finding.' The `IsBackground = true` line used twice in the ExclusiveContext code is exactly the kind of claim the foreground/background-threads doc could have supported but doesn't cite, and the ValueTask recycling claim ('some ValueTask implementations recycle their internal state as soon as they're consumed once') is closer to the uncited devblog post's subject matter than to the cited ValueTask Struct API page.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either cite each source inline where its claim is made (e.g. cite the foreground/background doc next to `IsBackground = true`, explaining why the pump thread is a background thread; cite the ValueTask devblog post next to the recycling/undefined-behavior claim) or remove the two sources from front matter if the claims they'd support aren't actually needed.

issues.location: Section '`ValueTask<T>`: paying for the box only when you need it', the sentence quoting '"the default choice for any asynchronous method... should be `Task`. Only if performance analysis proves it worthwhile should a `ValueTask` be used instead" ([ValueTask Struct])'
issues.problem: The live ValueTask Struct page's full sentence is 'the default choice for any asynchronous method that does not return a result should be to return a Task' — the ellipsis removes a qualifier that, read literally, scopes the guidance to the non-generic ValueTask (no return value), not the ValueTask<TResult> under discussion in this section. The underlying claim is still true (the ValueTask<TResult> page separately states the same preference for Task<TResult>), so this isn't a fabrication, but the specific citation doesn't support the generic-type claim as cleanly as the unelided quote implies.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either cite the ValueTask<TResult> Struct page instead (or in addition), which has its own near-identical sentence ('the default choice for any asynchronous method should be to return a Task or Task<TResult>. Only if performance analysis proves it worthwhile should a ValueTask<TResult> be used instead of a Task<TResult>'), or adjust the ellipsis/wording so it doesn't imply the non-generic page's sentence was written about the generic type.
